This is a very common issue with induction hobs, and while it can be frustrating, it is usually caused by one of three specific things: overheating protection, power limitation settings, or voltage instability.

Here’s a breakdown of the most likely causes and how to fix them:

### 1. Overheating Protection (Most Likely)
Induction hobs have built-in thermal sensors. If the internal fan can’t cool the electronics fast enough, or if the glass gets too hot from residual heat, it will shut off automatically to prevent damage.
• Why it happens on high: High power generates more heat in the unit itself.
• Check this:
• Ventilation: Are there objects blocking the vents (usually at the back or sides)? Ensure there’s at least 5–10cm of clearance.
• Fan Noise: Listen closely right before it shuts off. If you hear the fan ramping up to max speed, the unit is overheating.
• Glass Heat: Even though induction heats the pan, not the glass, the heat transfers from the pan back to the hob. If you’re using a very large or heavy pot on high for 10 minutes, the residual heat can trigger the sensor.

### 2. Power Limitation / "Boost" Mode Timer
Many modern hobs have a Boost function (maximum power) that is only allowed for a short time (usually 5–10 minutes). After that, it automatically reduces power to prevent overheating or tripping your home’s circuit breaker.
• Check this: Look at your manual. If you’re using "Boost" or the highest setting, try switching to a slightly lower setting (e.g., from Boost to 9/10) and see if it stays on longer. It might be designed to do this intentionally.

### 3. Voltage Instability or Loose Wiring
Induction hobs are very sensitive to voltage fluctuations. If your home’s electrical supply dips slightly under high load, the hob may shut off as a safety measure.
• Check this:
• Does it happen when other high-power appliances (oven, microwave, dryer) are running nearby?
• Is the hob hardwired or plugged into an outlet? If it’s plugged in, try a different circuit/outlet if possible. Hardwired units may need a qualified electrician to check for loose connections at the terminal block.

### 4. Faulty Temperature Sensor or Control Board
If none of the above apply, one of the internal components (like the NTC temperature sensor) might be failing and giving false readings, causing premature shutdowns.
• Check this: If the hob is under warranty, contact the manufacturer. If not, a repair technician can test the sensors with a multimeter.

---

### ✅ Quick Troubleshooting Steps:
1. Clean the vents around the edges of the hob.
2. Reduce the power level slightly (e.g., from 9/Boost to 7/8) and see if it stays on longer.
3. Ensure proper ventilation – don’t block air intake/exhaust holes.
4. Check your home’s electrical load – avoid using other high-wattage appliances simultaneously.
5. Reset the hob: Turn off the power at the circuit breaker for 1–2 minutes, then turn it back on. This can clear any temporary error states.

If it still happens after trying these steps, it’s likely a hardware fault (sensor or control board) and you’ll need a professional repair.

That confirms it: the fan roaring is your hob’s way of screaming for help. It has detected that its internal temperature is rising too fast and is shutting itself down to prevent permanent damage.

Since this started right after you installed a new drawer unit underneath, the culprit is almost certainly restricted airflow.

### Why This Happens
Samsung induction hobs (and most built-in models) pull cool air in from the sides or back and exhaust hot air out through vents at the rear or top. If that new drawer unit:
1.  Blocks the rear/side vents: Even a small gap can cause heat to build up inside the hob’s electronics compartment.
2.  Traps heat: Drawers are enclosed spaces. Heat from the hob (which gets hot on the surface) has nowhere to escape, creating a "oven effect" around the hob’s internal components.
3.  Vibrations: If the drawer unit is poorly fitted or vibrating against the hob, it might be slightly misaligning vents or causing heat transfer issues.

### What You Need To Do (Quick Fixes)
1.  Check Vent Clearance: Look at the back and sides of your hob. Are there any gaps between the hob’s edge and the new drawer unit? There should be a clear path for air to flow out. If the drawer unit is touching or very close to the vents, you need to create more space.
2.  Remove Items from Drawers: Avoid storing heat-sensitive items (like plastic containers) directly under the hob if possible, as this can trap even more heat.
3.  Use Lower Power Settings: Since airflow is compromised, avoid using "Boost" or the highest setting for extended periods. Use medium-high instead of max-high.
4.  Check for Debris: Sometimes installation dust or packaging material gets trapped behind the hob during fitting. If you’re comfortable doing so, carefully check around the edges for any obstructions.

### Important Note on Warranty
Since this is a Samsung hob and it’s likely still under warranty (especially if it’s new), do not attempt to open the unit yourself. Contact Samsung support or your installer:
• Explain that the fan roars before shutting off.
• Mention that this started after the drawer unit installation.
• Ask if they can send a technician to check for ventilation issues or internal faults.

If the airflow is physically blocked by the new cabinetry, you may need to modify the drawer unit (e.g., add vents to the back of the cabinet) to allow proper air circulation.
